items: Fan: one parent, two independent children — children multiply.
Symptom is inflated SUM/COUNT. Fix by pre-aggregating each child.
A lateral join works too.
Chasm: two unrelated many:1 paths meet at a shared dimension.
Chasm output rows correspond to no real fact at all.
Star schema is safe: fact LEFT JOINed to dims, each many:1.
Many:1 never multiplies — that is the whole design.

blocks.title: Count After Every Join
blocks.text: Add one join, check the row count. Unexpected change means the newest join is many:many. CTEs make a 9-table join read as three named 3-table steps, same semantics.

items: UNION stacks rows vertically and dedupes the whole combined set.
UNION ALL stacks and keeps everything, no comparison work.
UNION ALL is strictly faster — UNION needs a sort or hash pass.
Default to ALL; use UNION only when dedupe is genuinely required.
Both sides need the same column count, order, compatible types.
Output column names come from the first SELECT.
Dedupe treats NULL as equal to NULL — opposite of join predicates.

lines: (SELECT id FROM a ORDER BY id LIMIT 5)
ORDER BY id;   -- once, after last SELECT

items: Branch LIMIT needs its own parentheses.
Final ORDER BY uses output column names or positions.
It applies to the whole combined result, never one branch.

lines: SELECT 'active' AS source, id FROM users
-- tag branches so rows stay traceable

items: Uses: merging monthly or sharded tables.
Appending a synthetic 'Total' row to a report.
Combining two classifications of the same entity.

blocks.title: Two Sharp Edges
items: INT ∪ TEXT errors or silently coerces — cast explicitly.
UNION is not a replacement for OR in WHERE.
But rewriting OR as UNION ALL can give each branch its own index.
INTERSECT: rows present in both sets, deduplicated by default.
EXCEPT: rows in the first set not in the second (Oracle: MINUS).
Both compare the ENTIRE projected row, not a key column.
That misread is the most common misuse of either.
EXCEPT is not commutative; INTERSECT is.
NULLs match each other, so an all-NULL row counts as a duplicate.
MySQL only added both in 8.0.31 — before that, emulate with joins.
ALL variants use multiset semantics; Postgres has them.
MySQL and SQL Server do not.
Precedence: INTERSECT binds tighter than UNION and EXCEPT.
UNION and EXCEPT are left-associative — parenthesize when mixing.

lines: (SELECT * FROM a EXCEPT SELECT * FROM b)
(SELECT * FROM b EXCEPT SELECT * FROM a);

blocks.title: It Can Lie About Duplicates
blocks.text: EXCEPT collapses duplicates, so it reports 'identical' for tables with different row multiplicities. Use EXCEPT ALL, or compare COUNT(*) too. Day job: INTERSECT for audience overlap, EXCEPT for churn.

items: Joins widen: add columns. Set ops lengthen: add rows.
Ask which direction the data grows, then pick.
Shape mismatch is the fastest signal you grabbed the wrong tool.
UNION ALL has no join equivalent at all.

lines: -- A INTERSECT B  ==  semi-join, all cols
SELECT DISTINCT a.* FROM A a
WHERE b.k IS NOT DISTINCT FROM a.k);

items: EXCEPT ≈ anti-join: NOT EXISTS, NULL-safe on every column.
Comparing only some columns? Use a join or EXISTS.
INTERSECT/EXCEPT always compare the full row — wrong tool there.
Joins can multiply rows; INTERSECT and EXCEPT never do.
That determinism is why they suit set-membership questions.
But they sort or hash both inputs entirely.
A correlated NOT EXISTS can index-seek and stop early.
WHERE on the right table after a LEFT JOIN — move it into ON.
Many:many explosion then SUM: totals are exact multiples of truth.
COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN counts 1 for zero-order customers.
Use COUNT(o.order_id) instead.
NOT IN against a subquery holding NULL returns zero rows.
Missing a column in a composite key joins across tenants or dates.
NATURAL JOIN, then someone adds updated_at to both tables.

lines: ON UPPER(a.code) = b.code   -- no index seek
ON a.varchar_key = b.int_key -- cast per row
-- fix: normalize on write, or functional index

items: DISTINCT to paper over duplicates hides the real multiplying join.
It also buys you a sort you did not need.
Mixing UNION and EXCEPT unparenthesized: left-associative surprise.
Check row counts after every added join.
Compare against COUNT(DISTINCT primary_key).
Run the query with LIMIT on a known ID first.

blocks.title: Before You Ship
blocks.text: Run old query and new query through (A EXCEPT B) UNION ALL (B EXCEPT A). Confirm it is empty, then merge.

items: Index every foreign key column yourself.
The child side of a 1:many join is rarely indexed by default.
MySQL/InnoDB is the exception — it indexes FKs for you.
Composite column order must match the join's leading columns.
A covering index (join key + selected columns) skips the table lookup.
Select only needed columns — wide rows swell the hash table.
Wider build side means spills arrive sooner.
Run ANALYZE / UPDATE STATISTICS after bulk loads.
Otherwise the planner estimates against yesterday's data.
Push WHERE filters down so fewer rows enter the join.
Watch the plan for hash spills to disk.
Raising work_mem can fix a slow join with no query change.
Prefer EXISTS over IN for large subqueries with duplicates.
EXISTS short-circuits and never materializes the full list.
Replace repeated self joins for adjacent rows with window functions.
BETWEEN date joins cannot use hash — inequality blocks it.
Ensure a sorted index for merge join, or bound the range tightly.
Very large joins: denormalize, materialized views, partition-wise joins.
Measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, never plain EXPLAIN.
Estimated rows lie; actual rows do not.
INNER keeps intersections.
LEFT keeps A plus intersections.
FULL keeps everything.
ANTI keeps A minus intersections.
ON decides what matches; WHERE decides what survives.
On outer joins those are two different moments in time.
NULL never matches in a join.
NULL equals NULL in UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT, GROUP BY, DISTINCT.
All four compare whole rows and need identical column shape.
Nested loop: small outer plus indexed inner.
Hash: big equality joins.
Merge: pre-sorted inputs or inequality ranges.
Debug ritual: INNER first, count, widen to LEFT, read the delta.
That delta names your unmatched data precisely.

blocks.title: Reviewer Red Flags
items: A WHERE on a LEFT JOIN's right table.
NOT IN with a subquery.
Any NATURAL JOIN.
A DISTINCT that appeared right after a bug report.
UNION ALL over UNION. NOT EXISTS over NOT IN.
LEFT over RIGHT. Explicit CROSS over comma syntax.
Explicit ON over USING or NATURAL.
Also flag any join predicate wrapped in a function.

blocks.title: One Sentence Frame
blocks.text: A join is a filtered cross product plus an optional promise to preserve one or both sides. Everything in this handbook follows from that.

caption.text: Part 2 of SQL JOINS & SET OPS. Most SQL bugs don't crash — they quietly return the wrong number. A WHERE clause in the wrong place turns your LEFT JOIN into an INNER one, a many:many join triples your revenue total, and one NULL inside a NOT IN subquery wipes the whole result set. 10 pages: every join type, every set operator, the three execution algorithms, and the exact mistakes that corrupt results without ever throwing an error.
